back: A new or revitalised product is developed because of consumer demand — consumers want upgraded products with improved functionality.
Developments in technology, materials, components and manufacturing lead to new products being developed, e.g. smaller electronic components making wearable technology possible.
Designers and manufacturers must be sure consumers need a new product for it to succeed. Technology often drives consumer choice.

front: Four stages of the Product Life Cycle
back: 1. Introduction — product launched. 2. Growth — sales steadily increase. 3. Maturity — sales reach their peak. 4. Decline — sales drop off.

front: Why manufacturers use the Product Life Cycle
back: It is a marketing tool to judge when to increase or stop manufacture, or replace a product with a new or revitalised one.
When a product no longer sells, or only sells at a discount, because it is no longer desired. Manufacturers can build it in by replacing products in a set time frame.
Gives consumers greater choice and lower prices, and connects cultures through communication technology — but costs the environment, Western jobs, and can exploit people in developing countries.
The British Standards Institution sets standards for products sold in the UK. Products that meet BSI standards carry the Kitemark.
International Organisation for Standardisation — sets international standards for products and processes to ensure quality, safety and efficiency worldwide.
ISO 9001 is the quality management standard; ISO 14001 is the environmental management standard. They give consumers confidence a product is independently tested to be safe and of good quality.
All goods must be of satisfactory quality, as described, and fit for purpose. It covers faulty and counterfeit goods, poor service, contracts and online purchases including digital downloads.

front: How long do you have to reject faulty goods?
back: Normally 30 days for a full refund under the Consumer Rights Act. Shop returns policies for unwanted items go beyond the law and are voluntary.
Makes it illegal to apply a false description to goods that misleads consumers.

front: Social, cultural, economic and environmental responsibilities
back: Social — no unforeseen side effects on people. Cultural — acceptable and not offensive to a group. Economic — sound financial decisions (materials, profit, running costs). Environmental — meeting laws and targets such as lowering CO₂ emissions.
Unfair working conditions, such as poor or unfair pay and child labour, which can happen where employment laws are weaker.
Meeting today's needs without compromising future needs: using recycled or less material, renewable or less energy, extending product life, reducing waste and avoiding harmful substances.
Chlorofluorocarbons — once used in fridges and aerosols. They damage the ozone layer and are now banned.
